With GTA 6 auto drive you can sit back and take in the sights while Jason or Lucia make their own way to the destination

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By using auto drive in GTA 6 you get the opportunity to appreciate the level of detail your vehicle has, and how beautiful the world is around you, without the risk of slamming straight into the back of the next car as soon as you hit traffic. When you're not dealing with the controls yourself it can be quite relaxing to cruise around GTA 6, soaking up the sights and generally admiring everything Rockstar has created. To find out how it all works, here's how to enable auto drive in GTA 6.

To use GTA 6 auto drive, you need to be in control of a vehicle and have a destination marker set on your map. From the vehicle, hold Down on the D-pad to access the camera options, then while still holding it press Options (PS5) or Menu (Xbox) to enter the CINEMATIC menu. You'll then see a prompt for ENABLE AUTO DRIVE in the bottom right corner, so hold the appropriate button to get it started.

Jason or Lucia will then begin driving on their own towards the destination, as the camera cycles through various cinematic views. You can use the right stick to move the camera around, and click R3/RS to switch to the next view. The triggers will also let you choose between three driving speeds, to determine how fast your driver will go, and you can change the destination marker on the map at any time to reroute.

We need to be clear that this is certainly not fast travel in GTA 6, as Jason or Lucia will obey all road rules and spend a lot of time sat in traffic, so it is instead intended as a way to soak up the atmosphere and get some great video footage or screenshots of your journey.

Also, be aware that auto drive in GTA 6 doesn't make everything perfect, and when I used it another driver hit my car then got out and started attacking it with a wrench! If something similar happens to you, then here's how to repair and fix your car in GTA 6.

Unreal Engine 6 will not launch with the engine's long-standard Blueprints scripting system. The news came in a Friday, November 19 post on the Unreal Engine website, written by Epic Games executive vice president of development, Marcus Wassmer. Here's Wassmer's top-level summary from the post:

"UE6, including UE6 Early Access, won’t include Blueprints or the Actor Gameplay Framework. Gameplay will be built in Verse and on the new Scene Graph framework.

"In June, we said Blueprints and Actors would coexist in UE6 Early Access and 6.0, so UE5 projects could upgrade incrementally while the new Scene Graph framework matures. However, with recent advances in AI capability, we expect AI to massively help with converting UE5 projects to UE6, if not make that process fully automatic. That also means we can deliver UE6 on time (or sooner!) while meeting its design goals: a new data model, a Verse-first architecture, modularity, and AI operability."

Blueprints have not (and it appears, will not) be deprecated in Unreal Engine 5, and the company maintains that projects will still be easy to convert from UE5 to UE6. Wassmer cited a declining cost in AI task completion as one reason for this belief, as well as the team's ongoing, but apparently successful conversion of Fortnite's Blueprint library to UE6's Verse programming language through an AI-assisted process.

Blueprints are a widely-used feature of Unreal. Former Valve developer Chet Faliszek, an AI skeptic, has put out a vlog on the subject. Essentially, Faliszek argues that Blueprints (and features like them in other game engines) represent a middle ground between artistic and technical work, an introduction and skill builder for less technically-minded developers. Without them, such developers seemingly have to either learn Verse code, or integrate LLM prompting into their workflows.

"We made a new skill in the middle there, between normal and expert," Faliszek said of intermediate tools like Blueprints. "To lose that determinism from game design, and instead have to prompt AI⁠—or write your own Verse … It's losing those tools that made all those designers and all those artists so powerful, to be able to do really powerful things and have access to really deep-down things, but in a safe way that the engineers can decide what that meant to them."

A dark horse game of the year candidate, the first-person RPG Queen's Domain, was made with Unreal Engine. I recently spoke to co-developer Eric Berger, who specialized in art and design alongside the more technically-focused Bradley Boothe, a relationship that rhymes with the ones Faliszek outlined in his video.

I spoke to Berger before seeing Epic's latest press release, but Berger already indicated that Unreal's AI pivot is prompting Freshly Baked Games to switch engines for its next project. I followed up with Berger about this Blueprint news, and the developer said that Blueprints were a major part of the workflow on Queen's Domain.

I'm a layman in game development, but I think Wassmer's post elides that there is a large qualitative difference between doing any work via LLM prompt versus the old-fashioned way⁠—I don't like or want to use these tools, myself, and I don't think that's an unpopular stance. Commenter ZILtoid1991 on Faliszek's video compared the move to Apple removing headphone jacks on the iPhone, a comparison I find fruitful.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

It was hugely unpopular at the time, and is still derided by enthusiasts, but it also worked. Other manufacturers copied Apple, and everybody has bluetooth headphones now⁠—or Apple's own, proprietary Air Pods. But Apple had far less success trying something similar with its laptops: The lack of ports on late 2010s Macbooks proved disastrous, and Apple has since reintroduced more (and a wider variety of) ports on newer models of the popular line. I certainly have my own anti-AI, pro-headphone jack preferences, but we'll have to see how this plays out with the Unreal Engine.

You can choose whether to sell the coke cut with baby powder or the pure stuff for profitability in GTA 6 mission "Dealer's Choice"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The choice to sell pure or cut coke in GTA 6 comes around early in Chapter 3 as part of the "Dealer's Choice" mission, in which Boobie asks Jason to go get drugs from Tyrone and sell them on. Boobie seems happy for Jason to sell a less-than perfect product if it means higher profitability, but Dre'Quan has been warning you about overstepping constantly, suggesting that this might be less than wise. Below I'll explain all the outcomes of choosing the cut drugs or the pure stuff in Grand Theft Auto 6, as well as what the best choice actually is.

What appears to be a double choice in GTA 6 to sell the pure or cut drugs can actually split three ways, as selling the cut drugs leads to a second choice: when you get found out, are you still going to demand the same price for worse coke?

Here's all three outcomes in GTA 6, though keep in mind that any financial gain is earned later after the mission when Boobie sends your cut of the money to you.

We've yet to play out all the outcomes, but it seems as though the highest payment comes from selling the pure stuff, which is $1,500 - not a lot anyway. Nonetheless, we'll update this guide if we find out more.

The reality is that this is not a hugely significant choice beyond the possibility of a shootout. The money that Boobie sends you later doesn't seem to be significantly impacted and there's no long-term story impacts, though you can marginally increase your profits by looting any enemies you encounter on the third option.

Still, I would choose the first option and sell pure for the best outcome, as it's the cleanest. That being said, the differences in reward are so minor that if you're out to make money fast in GTA 6, this quest doesn't make a huge difference either way.

For a more significant choice, check out what happens at the end of the GTA 6 Bigfoot and Skunk Ape questline, and what you should do about it!

#3706. Over 2 million Xbox players in the UK and US reportedly used the 'New Zealand trick' to play GTA 6 early - that's more than a third of the country's population

We already knew there'd be a frantic clamour for GTA 6 this week, and we also knew plenty of players would be eyeing up Xbox's 'New Zealand trick' to get in on the action early. But it's now being reported that a whopping 2m UK and US players took advantage of the trick - which, for context, equals more than a third of New Zealand's actual population.

Here's a quick bit of background: Rockstar's regional release schedule meant GTA 6 launched at midnight on 19th November everywhere, local time. As such, New Zealand was the first country in the world to see the hugely anticipated game go live, thanks to timezones. And because Xbox players can make purchases on any regional store easily, simply by changing their console's country, understandably impatient sorts opted to become temporary virtual New Zealand residents in their droves (on PlayStation, the process requires a regional account and payment in local currency so is more finicky).

In fact, according to data analytics firm Ampere Analysis, the early demand was such that 1.5m Xbox users in the US and 600,000 UK Xbox players briefly went Kiwi for the occasion of GTA 6's launch. Other countries highlighted by Ampere include Canada, where 200,000 Xbox players took the New Zealand plunge, Brazil (200,000 players), and Mexico (100,000 players).

By contrast, just 100,000 PlayStation players in the US opted to dive in early, reflecting, as Ampere notes, "the ease of being able to switch country in the account settings on Xbox consoles." And here's all that info in graph form:

Amusingly, New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first."

Some hours later and the rest of the world can now finally, officially join in the GTA 6 fun, and it's a game worth playing. Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell called it an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in his five star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#3705. Korridor turns those Youtube ads for vertical mobile shooters into a new, "deeply strategic" genre, and I can't decide if it's lying

The electro-metal OST seems legit, at least

I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

Show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

Per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole new "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

In Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

The fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

Is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.

A bit of awkward timing, but the filmmaker makes some good points.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I can't imagine Home Alone fans expected this much Kevin McCallister news ahead of Thanksgiving. Macaulay Culkin is reportedly returning to act in the franchise that made him a household name. But just minutes before that story hit amid the 2026 movie calendar, Chris Columbus, the director of the first two movies, was explaining why he didn't think another sequel could happen. And Columbus has a pretty heartbreaking reason for that.

Per Variety, Columbus had no idea Disney was developing another Home Alone movie when asked about the franchise's future. Shortly afterward, reports surfaced about Culkin working with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg on a new installment. The project is in its early stages, with Rogen and Goldberg shaping the script and producing through their Point Grey banner. Columbus, however, kept coming back to one person who helped make the original movie such a Christmas staple:

Catherine, as I’ve always said, is 50% of ‘Home Alone.’ There’s the yin and yang of ‘Home Alone’: Catherine O’Hara and Macaulay Culkin. Without those two in the film, there is no film, because they create the emotional epicenter of that film.

He's got a point. We all remember Kevin setting traps for Harry and Marv, screaming after putting on aftershave and eating a ridiculous amount of ice cream. But the first film also follows a frantic mother trying to get back to the child she accidentally left behind. That film's final reunion is still one of my favorite parts, and the late Catherine O'Hara, who played Kevin's mother, Kate McCallister, is at least 50% of why it works so well. O'Hara died in January at 71, and Columbus believes her absence would be impossible to overcome. As he explained:

I think you potentially could still entertain the idea of doing another ‘Home Alone’ with the cast. Not any of these ridiculous follow-ups to the first. And I only say ridiculous because it’s weird with filmmakers. They don’t understand why that cast works so well. It’s always about the cast. It’s like ‘The Goonies.’ It’s about the cast.

Unfortunately, the reunion he pictured is no longer possible. That makes the timing of his interview particularly surreal. He continued:

It was really about Catherine and Macaulay, if anyone ever wanted to do a sequel, and unfortunately that can’t happen now.

As essential as O’Hara was to the success of the first two movies, the bumbling baddies also made the film unforgettable. I'm, of course, talking about the Wet Bandits, played by Daniel Stern and Joe Pesci. Columbus also wanted to make sure those two other actors got their due, adding:

Let’s not downsize Harry and Marv. Daniel Stern and Joe Pesci are the ultimate comic duo for that particular film. Everyone has tried in subsequent sequels to be as funny or as interesting as Dan and Joe, and they just had a chemistry that is undefinable. So you can’t do that.

I can’t argue with the longtime filmmaker. The subsequent installments have struggled to reproduce the burglars' chemistry. Persci and Stern are hilarious in these iconic roles and not one single actor in any of the follow-up movies holds a candle to their performances in both of the first two movies. Getting hit in the face with a paint can is only funny so many times, but those two made it an art form.

After Columbus directed 1990's Home Alone and 1992's Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, the series continued without Culkin in Home Alone 3, Home Alone 4, Home Alone: The Holiday Heist and 2021's Home Sweet Home Alone. None brought back the core pairing that Columbus considers essential, and you can feel their absence.

Fired Home Alone Star Sad ‘Every Christmas’ He Has To ‘Put Up’ With More Stories About What Happened

As for the new project, there's an interesting idea on the table. During a fan event in 2025, Culkin floated a potential sequel in which an adult Kevin is raising a son who locks him out of the house and turns his father's old tricks against him. Reports suggest the film could follow Kevin's perspective as a dad, although no final story or additional casting has been confirmed.

Variety also noted that Columbus enjoyed Culkin's recent Home Alone-themed McDonald's commercial and would love to work with him again. When the outlet contacted him after the sequel news broke, though, he declined to comment further.

I'm curious to see what an adult Kevin McCallister looks like in a new movie, especially with Culkin (who now watches the OG film with his own kids) involved creatively. I also understand why Columbus can't picture it without O'Hara. Anyone trying to bring Home Alone back has to contend with the fact that one of the people who made us care about Kevin is gone.

The entire Home Alone franchise is available to stream with a Disney+ subscription.

A choice (or two!) can lead to drastically different endings.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Please note, this guide contains massive spoilers for some of the endings of Grand Theft Auto 6. If you don't want to know what happens, please stop reading!

There are multiple endings to GTA 6, and not all the endings take place in the same location. One of the potential final scenes during the GTA 6 story mission, The End of the Road, takes place on a bridge in the Leonida Keys.

After discovering the cops are onto them, Jason and Lucia drive away from Cal's house and head to Brian's marina to find an airplane. The police quickly trap them on a bridge with a roadblock ahead and multiple cars behind them. Lucia wants to keep going but Jason thinks it's all over for them. The player is then given a choice, "Swim for it" or "No Surrender."

AGAIN, MASSIVE SPOILERS BELOW! STOP NOW IF YOU DON'T WANT TO KNOW THE ENDINGS!

Jason and Lucia decide Tomas is better off without them in his life. They drive through the roadblock, shooting at the cops. They're both shot to death and we see them dead in the front seat of the car, still holding hands. During the end credits, we see Tomas living happily with Lucia's aunt and her husband and children.

Jason and Lucia decide to jump off the bridge and swim to freedom.

However, a second choice appears once you've chosen 'Swim for it.' As Jason gets out of the car, a prompt for Lucia to 'Exit' the car appears. You can choose for Lucia to follow through with the plan by pressing the button, or change your mind and let the prompt expire.

A: 'Swim for it' and 'Exit': The couple will get out of the car together and walk to the edge of the bridge. Lucia jumps but Jason does not, letting himself get arrested by the cops. During the credits, Lucia signs the deal which keeps her free and sends Jason to prison. We see her bring Tomas to visit him, so Jason finally meets his son, though it's through glass.

B: 'Swim for it' and don't 'Exit': If you choose to swim for it but don't choose the 'Exit' prompt, Jason will get out of the car but Lucia will remain in the car. The police will open fire and kill them both. As with the No Surrender option, we see Tomas living with Lucia's aunt's family.

C: 'Swim for it' and 'Exit' (with $2 million in Buck Me savings): If you delayed the Protective Custody mission of GTA 6 until you had deposited $2 million in savings, the Swim for it and Exit choices will show the same results, but during the credits, Lucia uses the money to get Jason released from prison. Lucia picks him up at prison, and Jason meets Tomas and holds his hand.

Note: These are not the only endings to GTA 6. I've seen several more endings that do not take place on the bridge at all and don't involve these particular choices.

#3702. World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

And when I fall in love, will it be (WoW) Forever?

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. New players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

The original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as big as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an important byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

The changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn new tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually launched Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

As I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted plans designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

#3701. Ubisoft cuts jobs at major Assassin's Creed and Far Cry studios as its year of layoffs continues

Ubisoft has confirmed more layoffs as part of its previously announced operational "reset", this time affecting 166 employees at its major Montréal and Québec City studios - the teams responsible for game series including Assassin's Creed and Far Cry. It says the cuts are necessary "to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs."

GamesIndustry.biz reports the cuts - believed to equate to around four percent of the studios' total headcount - will impact employees working on projects either recently cancelled or significantly changed.

The publication also understands the cuts, said to primarily impact production and support roles at Ubisoft Montréal and Québec City, include members of Vantage Studios - Ubisoft and Tencent's joint development venture announced last October, which focuses on the publisher's biggest franchises, including Far Cry, Rainbow Six Siege, and Assassin's Creed.

In a statement provided to Eurogamer, Ubisoft confirmed it is, "reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations", adding: "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

"We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues," the statement continued. "We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources."

These latest job cuts are part of a "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" announced by Ubisoft in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

Since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

The knightly Bretonnia faction is getting a major refresh in Warhammer The Old World, and they're every bit as impressive as you'd hope from such a regal army.

In an update to the old range that has been kicking around for well over a decade, we're now getting fully remodeled Bretonnia Knights of the Realm on horseback – which can also be made as the junior Knights Errant – alongside brand-new Pegasus Knights. It's unclear when the models will launch (there's no chance of them appearing in this week's Black Friday Warhammer deals, so forget about that), but we do know they'll be available first in an Army Reinforcement box set.

New to The Old World? The best place to start is the 2026 Core Set, which provides everything you need to play: rules, dice, a battlemat, and two small armies. It's tricky to get hold of in the US right now (though I did find some stock at Amazon), but it's available at a discount in the UK via indie stores like Zatu.

Considering how we got a revamp of the skeletal Tomb Kings of Khemri recently, it makes sense that the Bretonnians would follow. These two factions were the first to be launched for Old World, after all. You can get a closer look via Warhammer Community's official reveal, but suffice to say they're utterly gorgeous – especially when lined up in serried ranks.

However, I'm most interested in what these models represent. Their existence after a string of major additions (those new Tomb Kings units, an entirely fresh range of Chaos models, and the Grand Army of Cathay) indicates just how seriously Warhammer takes The Old World – and presumably how popular it's been, considering the way it keeps receiving such generous updates. I can only imagine how costly such a major overhaul has to be, so getting one after another tells you a lot about the Old World's general health.

Seeing as The Old World's predecessor (Warhammer Fantasy Battles) was scrapped in favor of the smaller and lighter Age of Sigmar back in 2015, I'd say that's one hell of a comeback.

While we're talking fantasy, fans adore this Lord of the Rings card game, and it's probably one of the best on Middle-earth.

Seriously, what is going on with this season?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’m not sure if you’ve noticed, but Survivor 51 is running out of main characters. We’ve somehow lost four of the biggest, loudest and most vibrant personalities in consecutive weeks, and now, we’re suddenly left with a season that has a few main characters, a couple wacky side characters and a bunch of people who have been consistently deprioritized and underedited throughout the season. What is going on? How many of these castaways can actually even win?

Jeff Probst has said in the past that there’s no one size fits all winner’s edit on Survivor. That’s both true and misleading. The longtime host and showrunner is correct in that the winner gets a different story based on their personality and what happened out there (the underdog, the challenge beast, the social threat, etc), but there is one very consistent pattern we do see: screentime.

I’m not saying the person who wins every season is the person with the most confessionals or the person with the most sympathetic edit, but one recurring theme is that the winner is always a consistent and active part of the narrative. The show goes out of their way to give us their perspective on what’s going on because the ultimate payoff needs to feel earned and it needs to make sense. That’s just storytelling 101. If we want to know, for example, why someone on the jury does or doesn’t vote for them at the end, it helps if we’re given context and confessionals about their relationship.

Unfortunately, with nine players left in Survivor 51, there are a ton of players who just aren’t present enough in the edit to seem like viable winners. Seriously, let’s run them down real quick. Cristian has been a little more prominent lately, but he had two confessionals during the first four episodes combined. Despite allegedly being so close to Sharonda that he told her about Carter’s idol, we haven’t seen that relationship developed in the slightest. This season would make no sense if he won.

It also wouldn’t make any sense if Thien An won. She’s in last place in total confessionals amongst the players left by an absolute mile. Why? I have no idea. She seems to have great social relationships and is an engaging and sometimes cutting confessionalist when she does get a chance to speak, but she’s the least present character in many episodes for unclear reasons. Why would they do that if she won?

Mike and Eric have been much more present parts of the edit, but their storylines have both been about how much everyone else is annoyed with them. Eric has been getting a wacky theater kid edit that has included multiple montages of him talking and everyone else being annoyed by it. There have maybe been ten shots of characters literally rolling their eyes after he talks. Mike is a different version of the same situation. He’s been the subject of numerous confessionals from other players about how he’s a “bottom feeder” and impossible to work with. I don’t see why Survivor would portray its winner that way.

That’s four of the remaining nine players who have seemingly no chance, and I’m not sure Maggie is in a good spot either. She seems to be one of the most well-liked and dangerous players on the entire island. No one would vote for Mike during the Duos Challenge because he was paired with her, and Jelly has dropped confessionals about how she can win if she gets to the end. But the edit also gave her very little credit for Linnea, even though it was her plan, and she has just over half as many confessionals as Jelly does (24 to 46).

That leaves literally four players: Jelly, Devin, Sharonda and Carter. I’d normally write Carter off because he has two episodes with zero confessionals and no player since Survivor 41 has won with even a single zero confessional episode, but as you can see, we’re a little short on viable winner possibilities. I’m out here trying to make excuses for people’s edits and see some silver lining showing why they could win. I think Carter can win. He’s at least been pretty present during the majority of the season. We’ve gotten his viewpoint consistently, and we’ve gotten confessionals from other people that speak of him very highly.

So, yeah, Carter is a maybe, but really, that leaves us with Jelly, Devin and Sharonda. The Helicopter Alliance has been the most consistent narrative throughline of the entire season, which is why it makes sense that these three are at the top of the list. Jelly and Devin have, without question, been the main characters of 52 (at least since Brady left), and they’re dominating in screentime and confessionals at 46 and 45 respectively. That’s twelve more than Eric, who is in third place of those remaining thanks to a bunch of vampire analogies and references to his fiance Gina.

Sharonda is quite a bit behind with 29 confessionals. Like Carter, there are some concerns with her edit, as there have been stretches where she hasn’t been super prominent, but her content has been so overwhelmingly positive that I’m willing to give her a pass. I still consider her a very viable winner at this point, as she should come into further prominence in the edit once the other players find out she’s been secretly working with Devin and Jelly the entire time.

I don’t know who is going to win Survivor 52. There are three, maybe four viable candidates with Maggie and maybe Mike added in there as wild longshots. That’s a really small number of people in play for there being nine castaways left. In fact, it’s starting to feel a little like Survivor 49 where the entire fanbase was convinced one member of the Tres Leches alliance was going to win because they were the only people who seemed viable for like the entire second half of the game (apart from maybe Steven I guess).

Lack of winning edits aside and a few questionable twist-related decisions aside, Survivor 51 has been an absolute banger so far. Fingers crossed it’s able to stick the landing and fulfill its potential to be an all-time great season, whether one of these obvious contenders wins or not.

#3698. GTA 6 players are being abducted by aliens and knocked out by Bigfoot

Grand Theft Auto 6 has only been out for a matter of hours, and players have already tracked down a UFO in the woods and a Bigfoot in the swamps.

The UFO encounter is a random night-time event in Kelly County, on a dirt road near the Starlet Motel safehouse east of Port Gellhorn. You'll need to have finished the game's first chapter, and it's most reliable after 2am in-game.

As word spread late yesterday (18th November), it seems the event will kick off if you find a car at the side of the road with its headlights flickering, its trunk open, and clothes strewn around it. Follow the trail into the trees towards a blue glow, and you'll catch a UFO beaming down on a woman before it drops her and flies off. Head back to her car, as she requests, and the UFO returns for you. You apparently black out and come round three days later, and a bronze trophy called The Truth Is Out There should unlock.

You can seemingly trigger the event as either Jason or Lucia, and it isn't needed for 100 percent completion.

And that's not the only close encounter you can expect, either. YouTuber Lazarbeam bumped into Bigfoot on the afternoon of 18th November, hours before the game launched in the UK, while one Reddit user reported that they weren't quite sure what they'd stumbled on, titling their post "I think I found Bigfoot".

Leonida's version of Bigfoot is actually the Skunk Ape, Florida's own swamp cryptid, and it can be found in the swamplands near Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County as soon as free roam opens up. Listen out for a loud roar, then use Jason's tracking ability to follow it through the swamp. You may find it feeding on a deer carcass, while a second sighting has been reported south of Watson Bay.

Either way, the trail seemingly ends at a strange, human-like tree. Investigate it, and Jason blacks out, triggering a short cutscene in which the creature creeps up on him, as shown in this video. He later wakes near his vehicle, drenched in sweat. Save your ammo, though, as shooting at it won't do you any good.

Cryptids and aliens are, of course, something of a Rockstar tradition by this point. GTA 5's Mount Chiliad mystery kept players hunting for years, and Output Lag has already spotted two NPCs in a GTA 6 bar talking about goings-on there. Nobody has cracked a full Chiliad-style puzzle in the new game yet, but I'm sure that's just a matter of when, not if.

GTA 6 launched today on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, although some have been getting in on the action earlier as a whopping 2m Xbox players in the UK and US took advantage of the trick of changing their console's country. Even New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty. "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first."

Eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#3697. Rockstar firings tribunal hears closing statements, with judge promising to deliver a verdict "as quickly as I possibly can" - though it may take a while

The employment tribunal over Rockstar's firing of 34 workers last year has come to an end for now, pending a final verdict from the judge. Said judge hasn't offered a concrete estimate of when her judgement will arrive, but has reportedly asserted that she'll provide it "as quickly as [she] possibly can".

That's according to People Make Games' Chris Bratt, who's reported on the tribunal throughout the proceedings."I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case," he cited judge Lucy Wiseman as having said following closing arguments from Rockstar and the union representing the fired staff over the past couple of days. "What I will say is that I will use my best [endeavours] to get that judgement out as quickly as I possibly can."

Bratt reported that could mean anything from weeks to a few months of waiting, leaving the fired staff looking at more time in the limbo they've occupied throughout the tribunal.

To recap the arguments Wiseman will have heard, Rockstar accused the fired staff of leaking "confidential information on a public forum", while the Independent Workers’ union of Great Britain (IWGB) union have accused Rockstar of being motivated by union busting in letting the workers go. According to a previous report from People Make Games, discussion of a new company Slack policy in a union-run Discord server preceded the firings.

The fired devs haven't called for supporters to boycott GTA 6 - the game they were working on prior to being let go - in solidarity, but instead to consider buying specially-designed union t-shirts, the proceeds of which will go towards the workers' "Fighting Fund".

Devs still at Rockstar and the IWGB have formed the Rockstar Games Workers Union since their fired colleagues' tribunal proceedings began and are in the midst of a vote on union recognition as of writing.

Writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section this week, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte expressed that it's "hard not to worry about what the future holds" for developers at the studio, with the prospect of layoffs potentially happening now the big game is out the door concerning staff. Uriarte made clear that, as of the writing of his piece, Rockstar staff "have had no indication that layoffs are coming".

Over the last couple of weeks, some Nvidia users noticed their SSDs were taking a hammering, reporting their driver's log file was being overwritten constantly, sometimes to the tune of 30 GB every hour. Which obviously isn't great for the lifespan of the valuable SSD you've got it installed on.

Given the problem was caused by recent driver updates, rolling back to version 621.01 was the best solution until Nvidia could do something about it. Which they did, releasing a hotfix as version 621.35. It's not available in the GeForce app yet, but you can download it directly from Nvidia's site. Not that you should.

As users on the Nvidia subreddit are reporting, the problem persists. While the hotfix reduces the peak write rate and prevents it for a short while after reboot, it eventually creeps back in. One user reported that overnight the log file was still being rewritten by approximately 4.5 GB every hour.

So yeah, the best solution remains to roll back to version 621.01 and, as always with Nvidia drivers, to hold off on updating to the latest driver until it's been confirmed safe. If this ongoing saga sounds familiar, it's because the same thing happened to AMD's GPU drivers earlier this month. Maybe vibecoding driver updates and then vibecoding fixes for their inevitable bugs isn't the best way of doing things.

Faye will be in God of War's Amazon show – played by game actor Deborah Ann Woll

As announced by Amazon, Woll is once more playing Faye, after making her first appearance as the character – the mother of Atreus and longtime partner of Kratos – in flashbacks and vision sequences during 2022's God of War Ragnarok.

Woll joins Dave Bautista's Kratos and Callum Vinson's Atreus in a first season that will likely mirror much of 2018's God of War narrative – namely, how Kratos and Atreus journey on a quest to spread Faye's ashes.

Bautista replaced original Kratos actor Ryan Hurst after he suffered an injury during production, forcing cameras to stop rolling.

Woll will also portray Faye once more in next year's standalone game God of War Laufey, which sees her fight through the mysterious Everywhen to enact her plans to save Kratos and her son, Atreus. She's even accompanied by a mysterious talking cube, voiced by The Boys actor Jack Quaid. Naturally.

"I've known about this for nearly ten years, and I haven't been able to talk about it." Woll, who also said she wasn't put off by the negative response to the title, explained earlier this year at Game Con Canada (via CG Mag).

She added, "When [director] Cory [Barlog] brought me in to talk about doing Ragnarok and show me the 2018 game, he already had a poster for the Laufey game with me and a cube. A cube that's been there since the beginning. It's deeply a part of the lore."

As wild as it is to admit, I resonated with this.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Body is available to stream right now with a Netflix subscription, and when I learned it was about controversy surrounding a Catholic school, I had to check it out. As someone who attended a Catholic grade school and high school, I was eager to see how it was portrayed, and while things were a bit wilder than I remember, the show really nailed two parts.

For those curious but still want to watch for themselves, I'll keep this spoiler-free. All readers really need to know going in is that this series surrounds a Catholic school dance team, and what happens when an initiation prank goes too far and a student's life is in danger.

Project Hail Mary was called "blatant Catholic propaganda," as described by someone who never watched, and similarly, The Body is being vilified by groups of concerned Catholics who have not and likely will not watch it. As someone who did, I'll admit no one should go into this assuming it'll be a family-friendly adventure, but the parts that handle religion are done with lots of care.

I say this, especially, as a person who went through their teenage years in Catholic school. For many, your teens are going to be one of the most rebellious and potentially dangerous times of your lives. Imagine some of the wildest things you did in high school, and now imagine the feeling that you'll be eternally damned for it days afterward.

"Catholic Guilt," they call it, is shown in full effect in The Body. Obviously, there are people in this who deserve to feel guilty, but there are also cases in which we see characters feel immense guilt or shame for things that would otherwise be quite normal today.

Some of this is due to The Body being set in 2004, when things like LGBTQ+ relationships weren't as prevalent in pop culture and were largely frowned upon in Catholic schools. Pregnant teens at my high school weren't allowed to walk to get their diploma at graduation, and I couldn't imagine what would happen if someone were openly gay back then.

And yet these things happened, and these people existed. It's one of the things I love about The Body, and the way it navigates what would undoubtedly be a scary time for those individuals. Again, it was more extreme than anything I dealt with, but I know that feeling of guilt quite well.

I also think The Body does a great job of handling what goes down when something controversial does happen at a Catholic school. I can't get into specifics, but there was a controversy at my school so big that it received national attention, and the fact that it was a Catholic school only amplified the interest and headlines.

The Internet Can’t Stop Talking About People’s Mouths In Netflix’s The Christmas Switch. I Can’t Unsee It

Like the kids in The Body, a number of kids attending were from families of some renown. Families were willing to keep quiet about events occurring to protect their children, and the school was eager to let any controversy fade as quickly as possible.

There's certainly something to the added pressure of a Catholic school striving to be perfect. As The Body points out, any controversy draws the same critics who will immediately point to past incidents highlighted by the movie Spotlight. No one wants to be the person to bring added negative attention to the religion, but at the end of the day it's a high school full of rowdy teens just like any other.

I'm admittedly a lapsed Catholic, but I would say The Body was the best representation in media for the faith since Wake Up, Dead Man. In that, both deal with Catholicism, but not so much that they're openly mocking or blaspheming it. They're stories about the people who practice it, who are imperfect and flawed. I don't think teachers should show it in class, but it is worth a watch for those who are curious.

Check out The Body and other upcoming Netflix shows as 2026 winds down. With the holidays right around the corner, there's nothing like watching something controversial to spark some conversation at the family dinner table!

#3693. World of Warcraft: Forever has more weekly players than WoW has seen in 15 years, says Blizzard

World of Warcraft: Forever now has more people playing each week than World of Warcraft has seen in 15 years, according to Blizzard.

"Another fun statistic for you! #WoWForever has more people playing weekly than we've seen in World of Warcraft in 15 years!" executive producer and World of Warcraft vice president Holly Longdale posted. "Thank you all for joining us in Azeroth. We're doing this together, for Forever!"

Longdale was quoting a post from the official World of Warcraft account, which shared a batch of "By the Numbers" stats for the new edition.

Since it launched on 4th November, players have created 15,160,147 characters and 140,764 guilds, completed 1,480,343,357 quests, and defeated 9,786,925,806 enemies.

Another fun statistic for you! #WoWForever has more people playing weekly than we've seen in World of Warcraft in 15 years! Thank you all for joining us in Azeroth. We're doing this together, for Forever! 💙♾️ https://t.co/bMLQduLri2

They've also formed 71,309,889 parties, used 28,696,386 camping items, and there have been 28,938,569 PvP kills.

Collectively, we've died a lot, too - 196,851,761 times in total, with Archmage Arugal, the final boss of Shadowfang Keep, seemingly the deadliest boss.

"You're breaking records by the day!" the post read.

Earlier this month, Blizzard said WoW: Forever was the biggest launch in World of Warcraft history by peak concurrent players, and that it had brought in the highest number of returning players the game has ever seen.

Longdale added at the time that it had pulled in the most new players for a WoW launch in 15 years. It has since suffered its first controversy, though, with a now-fixed gold exploit.

Last week, players pieced together a hidden quest chain that leads to two special swords. At the time of writing, only one has been found, though progress continues in pursuit of the second.

The game has been out for just over two weeks now, and continues to prove popular among new and returning players.

#3692. Hour-long Total War: Warhammer 40,000 campaign stream shows off ship battle-less fleet management, makes clear how not ideal getting Space Marine armies killed is

"It would take them decades to recover from that"

Try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please. So ask the bosses of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, who're keen not to have their training workloads doubled because you're a crap general and have gotten a tight-knit force of uber-tough grunts killed unnecessarily, hope as they watch you play. This and other things have been emphasised by a fresh stream showing off over an hour of campaigning in the strategy warhammerer.

The stream showed off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss. Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

Each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

As the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of big ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more quickly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

"Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs said, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

As well as giving a spit-and-polish digital release to various Warhammer classics, antique D&D games, and the cult ellipsoid horror games in the Ecstatica series, SNEG has been bug-fixing a bunch of strategy games from years gone by and getting them up on Steam and GOG. The latest trio to appear on digital platforms are Theocracy, Soldiers at War, and Warlords 4: Heroes of Etheria.

Warlords 4 was the final turn-based game in the beloved series, with the RTS spin-off series Warlords Battlecry already two games deep by the time of its release in 2003. This updated version supports resolutions up to 4K, and incorporates community fixes and a community-made campaign. It's available on Steam and GOG.

Soldiers at War took the X-COM/UFO turn-based tactics formula—this was 1998, X-COM still had a hyphen—and applied it to World War II. You'd choose a squad of eight from your platoon of 32 each mission, fighting through a campaign that started in North Africa and ended in Germany, gaining experience along the way. SNEG's version supports 1280x720 widescreen resolution. It's available on Steam and GOG.

Theocracy narrowly beat Total War to the punch in March of 2000 with its mix of turn-based civilization management and real-time battles, tasking you with uniting Aztec tribes before the prophesied Spanish invasion. You're on the clock with 100 years to use diplomacy, trade, and warfare to bring together an empire that can stand the test of time. The updated version still has a resolution of 800x600, but uses FSR 1 to scale up for modern displays. You'll be shocked to learn, it's also available on Steam and GOG.

All three games are designed to be easy to run on modern Windows systems, and have cloud saves and achievements. I'm tempted by Warlords 4, which I didn't play at the time because I'd moved over to the real-time Battlecry games by then. But I've still got fond memories of Warlords 2 Deluxe, which had 60 different worlds so if you were tired of raising griffon armies in its generic fantasy land you could conquer something oddball like Dante's Inferno instead. Or even make your own, right down to pixel-crafting the unit art. Good times.

#3690. Infamous GTA 6 leaker CyberLeek is back, and this time the group claims to have leaked a full development build of the game

CyberLeek, the persona of a hacker group that was responsible for leaking GTA 6 gameplay before the game launched, has reappeared today, claiming to have released a development build of the final version of the game on its site. This new leak appears to be making good on a threat posted back in October, where the group stated its intent to release a full, playable build of the game.

Various social media accounts have visited the site and noted the size of the download offered by CyberLeek is, indeed 209GB. Eurogamer has seen the site and can confirm this is what the group has claimed, however I have been unable to verify the existence of any actual files. On the site, CyberLeek claims this build is from November 2026 - meaning it is very close to (if not the actual) release build. The 'executable file appears to be missing from the build, however, meaning you cannot actually - yet - get it up and running. CyberLeek is threatening to release this file at a later date, however.

"It is done," a statement from CyberLeek reads. "[Cyberleek] holds the full November 2026 build of Grand Theft Auto 6, and it is going out by torrent. Now. Every file except one. The main executable is held on a countdown." CyberLeek says the executable will be released earlier than planned if its crypto token reaches a predetermined value. Many of the leaks to date have been related to a CyberLeek crypto scheme. Previously, it was estimated that the group cashed out at least £200,000.

What does all this mean? There's a very realistic chance that the game could be up and running on PC soon - undercutting Rockstar's unannounced PC release by a matter of months, if current rumours are to be believed. "This community will have it emulated inside a week, running far past 30fps," the statement continues. "[CyberLeek] told you not to preorder for a reason. This is one of the reasons.

"If the Xbox build cannot be made to work and support holds, [CyberLeek] will work to get a PS5 build - a fallback, most likely never required. Either way: the Xbox build is going out. No double dipping for Take-Two/Rockstar." It seems these are not empty threats.

CyberLeek has been a thorn in Rockstar's side for a while now. The group initially claimed it took this action in the name of "Gamers' Rights", supposedly fighting for consumers in relation to the controversial discontinuation of game-discs and the digital-only future being pursued by game publishers. Rockstar has previously issued statements regarding the leaker, noting that the leaks are "heartbreaking" and that "this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time". Take-Two tried to subpoena Discord for information pertaining to the leaker's identity.

Xbox Project Helix, the next (mysterious) console underway from Microsoft, has been in the limelight recently for its support of PC games – support that was reportedly far more fleshed out during the hardware's initial conception.

Jason Ronald, vice president of Xbox's gaming devices and ecosystem team, recently said that Project Helix is "a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC," as "it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine." That sounds pretty dang capable already, but apparently, it was supposed to feature even more PC integration – think full-on free online multiplayer access, Steam, and the like.

Anonymous sources tell Windows Central as much, alleging that the original plan – one operating underneath a different codename – for the console was for it to essentially be a gaming computer that can also run Xbox games… on top of PC titles on storefronts like Valve's own Steam. Think the ASUS ROG Xbox Ally, for example, albeit not handheld. I'm reminded of the Steam Machine, personally, although that notably doesn't run on Windows.

The supposed predecessor to Project Helix would work with a gamepad-centered Xbox-style full-screen interface (like Steam's Big Picture Mode, for example), allowing users to exit out to a normal Windows desktop and run other programs such as Steam.

Furthermore, the report states the console would've been free to play online – no extra subscriptions or fees like Sony's PlayStation Plus service required to engage in multiplayer games.

That would mean no Xbox Game Pass paywall, as a PC wouldn't… well, work with a paywall at all, really. This wouldn't have been a cheap decision for Microsoft, and that paired with a move toward another hardware strategy, changes in management, and more, likely contributed to a reshuffle of plans – if this intriguing computer-esque console ever truly was on the table, that is. It does all beg the question: what will Project Helix look like?

I suppose we won't know until it's finally here. Let's just hope it doesn't cost as much as $1,800 – one rumored price point I can't quite get out of my head. For now, I think I'll just stick to my good ol' actual PC.

#3688. Ubisoft says Assassin's Creed Jade is still alive as it merges two of its Creative Houses

Ubisoft has confirmed that while Assassin's Creed Jade - its mobile entry in the series - is still in development, its focus remains with console and PC.

Speaking during the earnings call for Ubisoft's first-half results, CFO Frédérick Duguet said mobile was "still an opportunity for the medium to longer term, with games such as AC Jade on Assassin’s Creed", according to a transcript of the call published by Investing.com.

"Looking at what we can see in terms of long-term financial return, in the mindset of having a stronger focus in terms of capital allocation and financial returns, we consider that we would rather put our resources on bigger opportunities," Duguet said. "Today, we can say that console and PC remain our core focus for our biggest franchises."

He added: "The focus is really to make sure that we come with strong growth on console and PC, and notably PC, which is a more dynamic platform than ever."

Ubisoft last confirmed its China-set mobile game was still in the works in March, when it was mentioned in the publisher’s Assassin's Creed: Into 2026 blog. Assassin's Creed now sits within Vantage Studios, Ubisoft's joint venture with Tencent, which launched last year.

Ubisoft's results also confirmed some more changes to the way the company is run, with the publisher saying its new operating model is "now fully in place". Creative Houses 3 and 5 have been combined under the leadership of Julien Bares "to leverage synergies between Live experiences across platforms".

All leadership roles across the Creative Houses are now filled, too. An external general manager has been appointed for Creative House 4 and is set to join in January 2027, though Ubisoft hasn't yet confirmed who. That follows September's appointment of 2K and Amazon Games veteran Christoph Hartmann to lead Creative House 2, home to The Division, Ghost Recon, and Splinter Cell, which was renamed Massive Entertainment at the same time.

Outside the Creative Houses, Motherbrain, the team behind Ubisoft's generative AI experiment Teammates, is now a subsidiary in its own right. It's working on "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds". A separate unit has also been set up to look after brands that don't belong to any of the Creative Houses.

Ubisoft says the new structure is already paying off, pointing to the commercial success of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced and renewed momentum for Rainbow Six Siege, which it says ranked among the top 10 games across Xbox and PlayStation for monthly active users over the half.

That said, the publisher nonetheless posted a net loss of €254.5 million for the first half of the year, with net bookings down 16.5 percent to €644.7 million.

The news comes just hours after Ubisoft confirmed 166 job cuts at its Montréal and Québec City studios, the latest in a year of layoffs. They're part of the "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" that Ubisoft announced in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

Since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

On the weekend, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on a new Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

The 90 Day Fiancé family has sadly lost yet another beloved member. Sheila Mangubat, who appeared on Season 6 of Before The 90 Days, has reportedly passed away at 35. News of Mangubat's passing first arrived via her former fiancé, David Dangerfield, who shared the news with all of his followers by way of a heartbreaking statement.

David, whom viewers saw travel to the Philippines to see Sheila, posted his message on Instagram. Just months after announcing that he and Sheila were back together after an on-and-off romance, David shared the news as follows:

It breaks my heart to share the news from her family that Sheila passed away on Saturday in the Philippines. I am devastated and still trying to process this loss. Please keep her son, her family, and me in your prayers. Thank you for all your love and support. ❤️🕊️

Further details about Shelia's passing arrived via 90 Day insider Shabooty, who found a comment from a friend who said she passed away from uterine cancer. It should be mentioned as of this writing, Sheila's family has not confirmed her official cause of death. There was a level of skepticism from others online, given the lack of an official obituary though, so far, reported evidence seemingly points to this information being accurate.

Prior to this news, there was no mention that Sheila was sick or battling cancer. That fact was what apparently sparked the skepticism from fans regarding the initial claims and led to investigations from other accounts.

Two Updates On 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way's Andi And Nigel Have Me More Confused Than Ever About Their Relationship

90 Day Fiancé fans may remember David (who is deaf) finding love with Sheila and traveling to see if a life together was possible. Almost immediately, they were hit with tragedy, as her mother died after falling down a stairwell just hours after his arrival. Because of the tragedy, David and Sheila arguably weren't in the right mindset to really explore a future relationship and talk about the possibility of her being an eventual father to her son, Jhonreil.

There were other issues between the two, such Sheila being unable to understand or speak American Sign Language. Her misunderstanding presented an obvious communication barrier that neither of them considered before becoming involved. Still, they remained together, and it was even rumored ago that Mangubat was pregnant.

Ultimately, David wanted to bring Sheila to the United States with her son to live with him. Unfortunately, there were issues with the K1 visa process, and there were also financial struggles on his own end amid his attempts to get both of them to the US. That situation led to a brief breakup between them in late 2025, but as mentioned, the 90 Day couple later reconciled.

Fellow 90 Day Fiancé cast members reached out to David after he confirmed Sheila's death, including fellow Before The 90 Days Season 6 alum Tyray Mollett. Plenty of fans also expressed their condolences, and I think there was hope that we'd eventually see David and Sheila return in a future season. At this time, their storyline remains available to stream with an HBO Max subscription.

CinemaBlend offers its condolences to Sheila Manguat's family and friends and wishes them well during this difficult time. Here's hoping for more support and love from the 90 Day community as they continue to navigate this sad situation.
